wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e111.summary: Poses the final question of the Prologue: whether the theological habit is practical or speculative. Three arguments for speculative. (1) Per Ethics VI, the scientific part of the soul concerns necessary things and the calculative part contingent ones, and theology concerns necessary things. (2) Every speculative science is nobler than every practical one, because when a genus is divided, every member of the nobler species is nobler than every member of the other. Nothing speculative is nobler than theology, so theology is not practical. (3) Many theological truths are also metaphysical, and metaphysics is speculative.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e157.summary: Argument to the contrary: knowledge that directs voluntary operation is practical. Theology is such, since the wayfarer needs direction in fulfilling the divine commands, and only theology provides it.
claims: Knowledge directing voluntary operation is practical.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e168.summary: First opinion: theology is simply speculative. As moral science, though it considers truth, is called practical because it aims at doing good, so theology is called speculative because any work in it is for the sake of speculation. All practical sciences are ordered to speculative ones and the active life to the contemplative. Although theology can often be called practical because it considers operables, it should simply be called speculative.
claims: Theology is simply speculative because it is ordered to contemplation (reported).
All practical sciences are ordered to speculative ones (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e190.summary: Others' argument for that conclusion: the act of love by which the will unites itself to God is not praxis, so knowledge extending to it is not practical, and theology extends only to that act.
claims: The act of love uniting the will to God is not praxis (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e204.summary: Proof that this act is not praxis, from Metaphysics XII: the first mover moves as loved and desired, so the heaven (with its moving intelligence) moves as loving and desiring, to be assimilated to the first mover. Assimilation happens above all through the beatific act of loving. But for Aristotle beatitude consists in speculation, so the act of love is speculation, not praxis.
claims: The first mover moves as an object of love (reported).
Beatitude consists in speculation (reported).
The beatific act of love is speculation, not praxis (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e226.summary: Further, the Commentator on Ethics X: the happy person is akin to God through the intellect by extension to loving God, and happiness consists in speculation.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e233.summary: Further: ultimate happiness is speculative, not practical, yet includes acts of both will and intellect. Augustine (De Trinitate XII) places wisdom and the image of the Trinity in the higher portion of the soul, the contemplative part. That portion contains memory, intellect and will, the parts of the image, so enjoyment and love belong to the contemplative part.
claims: Ultimate happiness includes acts of both will and intellect (reported).
The higher, contemplative portion of the soul includes the will (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e257.summary: Further: if love of God were praxis, metaphysics would be practical, since love terminates in God under an essential, not a personal, ratio, and metaphysics considers the divine essentials more than our theology considers the notional.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e270.summary: Further: metaphysics considers God's goodness and so his lovability. If extension to love made a science practical, metaphysics would be practical.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e279.summary: Further: God is found in three genera of cause (formal, efficient, final), so he moves as loved and as end. If metaphysics considers this, it would be practical.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e293.summary: Further: as our theology directs love of God supernaturally, a natural science directing love of God, such as philosophers had, is possible. That science cannot be practical, because then a naturally acquired practical science would be nobler than every natural speculative science, against Aristotle. Just as supernatural love of God is nobler than supernatural knowledge (charity than faith), natural love is nobler than natural knowledge, so the habit directing it would be nobler.
claims: A naturally acquired practical science cannot be nobler than all speculative sciences (reported).
Charity is nobler than faith (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e322.summary: Further: theology is not about a doable or makeable object.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e327.summary: Further: every practical habit perfects the practical intellect, which concerns only what can be otherwise, and theology does not.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e336.summary: Ockham argues against the first opinion. There can be simply practical knowledge of a simply practical truth, just as there is speculative knowledge of any speculative truth, whether knowledge is called practical from its object or from its end. Many purely theological truths are simply practical ('God is to be worshipped in such a way', 'one should help one's neighbor for God's sake'). Only theology can know them, since no naturally discovered science concerns them, so theology is simply practical in that respect.
claims: There can be practical knowledge of any practical truth.
Truths like 'God is to be worshipped' are simply practical.
Such truths belong only to theology.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e386.summary: Objection: this consideration of works exists only for the sake of contemplating eternal things, to which it is ordered. Since that is speculative, this is too, especially since theology is one science.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e397.summary: Ockham argues that theology is not one science: distinct truths, one of which can be known without the other, have distinct sciences, and one can know a theological truth without ever thinking of another. Against the reply that theology is numerically one but heterogeneous (so parts can be acquired separately or conflict with different things): nothing is heterogeneous except where there is specific distinction or parts of different kinds. Animals are heterogeneous through specifically distinct accidents in different parts. A composite of matter and non-ultimate form like fire is not properly heterogeneous, since matter and form are not properly in a genus or species. Man would be heterogeneous if organs had distinct substantial forms.
claims: Theology is not one science, since its truths can be known separately.
Heterogeneity requires specifically distinct parts.
Fire is homogeneous though composed of matter and form.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e459.summary: If theology were a numerically one heterogeneous quality, it would be so in one of two ways. (1) Informed by specifically distinct accidents, as an animal's organs are: these cannot be relations to distinct conclusions, since conclusions are beings of reason with which no real relation is possible. A new real relation arises only through acquiring an absolute thing or local motion. Error about a conclusion is absolute, so its contrary is absolute. So the parts are absolute, and being permanent they are habits, specifically distinct for distinct truths. (2) Composed of parts of different kinds making a per se unity, so that one is act and the other potency: then a quality would have matter and form, though accidents have only matter in which, not out of which (Metaphysics VIII). A per se individual of one species cannot be an essential part of another species. So specifically distinct items make one only as many men make one kingdom or army.
claims: No real relation to a conclusion is possible, since conclusions are beings of reason.
A new real relation arises only by acquiring something absolute or by local motion.
Error is an absolute quality, so its contrary is absolute.
Accidents have no matter out of which they are composed.
Specifically distinct habits form one only as an aggregate, like an army.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e535.summary: Further arguments. By the same reasoning all sciences would be one heterogeneous quality. Heterogeneity requires parts of different kinds distinct in place and position, in determinate number by the common course of nature (animals, plants), and this quality's parts are not distinct in place. The part would not be named by the whole, so the habit of one conclusion would be no science, or a 'monstrous' one, like a man born with one hand. Ordering to contemplation does not make the science speculative: on the opponent's own view practical knowledge first concerns the work however it is further ordered, as practical sciences ordered to speculative ones remain practical. Theology is also not simply speculative, because it considers our works in our power; love of the end has been shown to be praxis; and the will can act well or badly concerning God, so there is practical knowledge of God regarding merit and demerit. A second opinion holds theology is simply practical. A priori, from its object: a habit is purely practical if its object can be attained by nobler operations than the habit's own acts. God is attained by faith, vision, charity and obedience, nobler than understanding what is believed (as being healthy beats knowing health, Ethics II). A posteriori, from its end: theology directs the act of believing, which it defends (Augustine). A third opinion (the Subtle Doctor's) agrees: practical extension consists in conformity to and natural priority over praxis. Theology's first object is conformable to right volition and naturally determines the intellect to know the rightness of praxis before the will wills, and the ultimate end yields practical principles. Ockham objects that practical knowledge concerns our works in our power, but 'God is three and one', 'God is omnipotent', 'God generates' do not, yet are theological. Against the reply that 'God is triune' virtually contains the rightness of loving three persons: then every truth would be practical ('man is in God's image', 'gold is inanimate'), and since on that doctor's view one subject cannot have both speculative and practical knowledge, the science of the soul and metaphysics would be practical. 'God is one', 'God is infinite' would be practical, so metaphysics would be practical in principles and conclusions. Against 'God is operable because attainable by our acts': angels, gold and all intelligibles are attainable by love. Ockham's own answer: theology is not one knowledge but contains really distinct cognitions, some simply practical and some speculative. Knowledge with neither praxis nor its product as object is speculative. Knowledge with praxis or its product as total or partial object, more directive than incomplex knowledge, is practical. 'God creates', 'God is triune', 'the Father generates' are speculative; 'God is to be loved with the whole heart', 'the Sabbath is to be sanctified', 'one should pray at the right place and time' are practical. Confirmation: knowledge agreeing with right appetite is practical. A first doubt follows: a habit without evidence from its object is not distinguished by its objects, or there would be two infused faiths.
claims: Heterogeneous composition requires parts distinct in place and position.
Ordering to contemplation does not make practical knowledge speculative.
Theology considers our works and so is not simply speculative.
If virtual containment of rightness made knowledge practical, every truth would be practical.
'God is triune', 'God creates', 'the Father generates' are speculative truths.
'God is to be loved with the whole heart' and similar truths are practical.
Theology contains really distinct cognitions, some practical and some speculative.
concepts: theology partly practical and partly speculative

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e896.summary: Continues the first doubt. This might be said of theology as handed down in Scripture, but not of theology in itself, whose object is the divine essence as this essence. Of that subject, being most truly one knowable, there is naturally first one truly unified knowledge, and whatever concerns something else first is not theology in itself. Also, the order of sciences by evidence stops at one, since two cannot be equally first, and that one is theology, which alone first concerns theology's first subject.
claims: Theology in itself has the divine essence as this essence as its subject (objection).
There is one first, unified knowledge of the divine essence (objection).

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e925.summary: Second doubt: when a practical conclusion is proved from speculative principles, there can be one habit, as one act, for the whole demonstration. Is it speculative or practical? Third doubt: does this practical theological habit belong to one of Aristotle's genera of intellectual habits in Ethics VI?

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e941.summary: Fourth doubt: should this practical habit be placed in the speculative or the practical intellect?

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e954.summary: Fifth doubt: which of these habits, the speculative or the practical, is nobler?

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e962.summary: Answers the first doubt: the habits are distinct, since experience shows one is acquired before another. The distinction is as great now in the wayfarer as it would be if theological habits were acquired without infused faith, with distinct habits for distinct knowables and believables. Also, faith and science are distinct, and theology has scientific habits for some truths and only faith for others. Whether a habit has evidence from its object makes no difference to its distinction: a heretic who believes one article and then others by acquired faith has distinct habits, since error about one article coexists with faith about another. Otherwise one habit of faith would cover all articles, histories and deeds believed, which is false. It does not follow that there are two infused faiths, only two acquired faiths, explained in Book III. On theology 'in itself': there is no theology except in some intellect. In the blessed, who have evidence from the object, there are or can be distinct habits, since one who sees the divine essence need not know that God is incarnate or is to be worshipped in the sacrament and could later acquire such a habit. The subject can be the divine essence, but one subject can have distinct cognitions through distinct predicates, as earth is studied both by natural science and by agriculture. Even if there is a first knowledge of the divine essence, further theological knowledge can follow, as 'earth is hard' precedes 'earth can be ploughed with hard iron', one speculative and one practical.
claims: Theological habits are distinct, as shown by their separate acquisition.
Having or lacking evidence from the object does not affect the distinction of habits.
A heretic has distinct acquired faiths for distinct articles.
There are distinct acquired faiths but not distinct infused faiths.
Theology exists only in some intellect.
Someone seeing the divine essence need not know that God is incarnate.
One subject can be known by distinct habits through distinct predicates.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e1112.summary: Objection to the reply: then faith regarding some articles could remain in heaven, in habit and act. Since ignorance of one thing coexists with any knowledge of another, faith about it can coexist as well. So one could see the divine essence and still have an act of faith that God is incarnate.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e1132.summary: Further objection: then theology would not be practical, since a blessed person knowing that God is to be loved supremely by the wayfarer does not have practical science, just as I knowing that the heaven is to be moved by an angel would not.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e1143.summary: Further objection: knowledge not about God as subject is not theological. 'God is to be loved supremely', 'God is to be worshipped', 'God is to be obeyed' are not about God as subject, since the subject is what really receives what the property imports, and man receives the love. So these belong to the science of man, not of God.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e1165.summary: Answers the first objection: it is not contradictory that one seeing the divine essence has faith that God is incarnate without evident knowledge of it, knowing it no more evidently than we do now. Such a person can lack intuitive cognition of the assumed nature and so cannot evidently know whether it exists or is united, and can simply believe it. Whether faith in fact remains in heaven for some articles, and whether faith can coexist with evident knowledge, is left to Book III.
claims: It is not contradictory that one who sees the divine essence believes the Incarnation without evidence.
Seeing the divine essence does not entail intuitive cognition of Christ's human nature.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e1194.summary: Answers the second objection: granting that a blessed person knowing that God is to be loved by the wayfarer lacks practical science, a blessed person knowing that God is to be loved supremely by that blessed person has practical knowledge, and it is theological. That suffices.
claims: Knowledge that one oneself should love God supremely is practical and theological.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e1208.summary: Answers the third objection: granting that God is not the subject in the strictest sense in 'God is to be loved...' (these are not proper predications, since what is apt to be subject is not subject), they should be recast as 'man should love God with his whole heart', 'man should obey God'. These are still theological, since science requires a predicate as well as a subject. Whether God is on the subject side or the predicate side, such truths are theological, especially since they cannot be naturally attained.
claims: Propositions like 'man should love God' are theological whether God is subject or predicate.
A science concerns predicates as well as subjects.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e1243.summary: Such truths can belong both to the science of man and to the science of God, since one is on the subject side and the other on the predicate side, as 'every man is risible' belongs to the science of man and of the risible. On the doctor's third argument: granting a first science of the first conclusion, there are other theological habits, as not only the first conclusion of geometry is geometrical. Second doubt answered: a single habit covering a speculative principle and a practical conclusion is formally neither speculative nor practical, in the sense in which these are opposites, but equivalently both, as the habit covering principles and conclusions is equivalently understanding and science and properly wisdom. There is no proper name for it. Objections: knowledge with our work as partial object is practical; knowledge perfectly and immediately directing work is practical; and speculative/practical is an immediate division of science.
claims: A truth can belong both to the science of its subject and the science of its predicate.
Theology has many habits beyond a first one.
A single habit of speculative principle and practical conclusion is equivalently both speculative and practical.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e1308.summary: Answers the first objection: knowledge with only one complex as object, part of which is a work, and directive of work, is formally practical. With several complexes as total object, it is practical only equivalently, being as useful for executing the work and as perfectly known as properly practical knowledge. If 'practical' means any knowledge about our work and directive of it, then 'speculative' and 'practical' are not opposites but can belong to the same thing, like 'productive of grass' and 'productive of worms' in the same sun. The same science would then be speculative (knowing a speculative principle or conclusion) and practical (knowing a practical conclusion). Aristotle uses the first sense.
claims: Knowledge of a single complex involving a work and directing it is formally practical.
Knowledge of several complexes is practical only equivalently.
In a broad sense 'speculative' and 'practical' are compatible, like two productive powers of the sun.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e1347.summary: Answers the second objection: all knowledge that perfectly and immediately directs a work is practical equivalently in the second sense, not in the first.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e1363.summary: Answers the third: there is a middle between speculative and practical science, since in the first sense they are not opposites. What is equivalently both lies between them, as wisdom lies between understanding (habit of principles) and science (habit of conclusions).
claims: There is a middle between speculative and practical science, namely a habit that is equivalently both.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e1376.summary: Answers the third doubt: the practical theological habit, like the speculative, is either evident or not. Evident: knowing that each is to be given his due, or that evil is not to be returned for good. Inevident: knowing that Christ's body in the sacrament is to be adored. The inevident habit belongs to none of the habits of Ethics VI, which concern evident acts. The evident one belongs to science (if science there includes practical science) or to prudence (if not), as Book III will explain.
claims: Practical theological habits are either evident or inevident.
'Each is to be given his due' is evidently known.
Inevident practical habits fall outside Aristotle's intellectual virtues.
Evident practical habits belong to science or prudence.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e1412.summary: Reports an answer to the fourth doubt: the practical theological habit is in the speculative intellect, not the practical. No habit proceeding from universals and acquired by reasoning is in the practical intellect, whose object is singulars and whose mode is experiential. Habits in the practical intellect are experiential and about particulars, as experts without art have (Metaphysics I). This habit is rational and from universals.
claims: The practical theological habit is in the speculative intellect (reported).
The practical intellect concerns singulars experientially (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e1438.summary: The opinion explains that the practical intellect is the particular reason and the speculative intellect the universal reason. For any operable, the particular reason forms an experiential habit by repeated acts and the universal reason a demonstrative one, so every science of operables divides into practice (experiential, in the practical intellect) and theory (from universals, in the contemplative intellect), as in medicine. The experienced operate better than theorists. Ockham replies that the dispute is more verbal than real, since words are by convention, and turns it against the opinion: the intellect can have a habit of a purely speculative singular (this eclipse at this time), which by their identification would be in the practical intellect, and universal habits are acquired by experience (Metaphysics I, Posterior Analytics II). Their principle is false: a habit from universals that is not directive is in the speculative intellect, and if directive, in the practical. Aristotle's 'contingent' object refers to the deliberative intellect, which concerns what is in our power, not to the practical intellect generally. Ockham's own view: the intellect is one and the same for all habits and acts. 'Speculative' and 'practical' intellect are denominations from habits, like 'white milk' and 'sweet milk'. When an intellect has both habits, whatever is in one is in the other, while 'this habit is in the practical intellect' can be false by false implication if it has no practical habit. 'A speculative habit is in the speculative intellect' is per se in an extended sense, while 'a practical habit is in the speculative intellect' is per accidens, like 'dry wood is white'. Against the opinion's other claims: the practical intellect's objects include universals as well as singulars; strictly speaking it concerns necessary and speculable things too, being the same intellect, though immediately directing it concerns singulars. 'Experiential' can mean habits taken immediately or mediately from intuitive cognition, and many of the latter are universal; in either sense not every practical habit is experiential. A universal habit directs immediately but only partially, as the builder's art needs knowledge of particular wood and stones. If the artisan knows everything the expert knows and no bodily habit is needed, the artisan works as well. Medicine contains purely speculative parts serving as principles of practical conclusions. Fifth doubt: a habit is nobler only by its subject, certainty or evidence, so an equally evident speculative theological habit ('God is infinite, the highest good') is nobler than a practical one ('God is to be loved'). Against the argument that the practical habit understands more (God and creatures), nobility of an incomplex object does not establish this; greater nobility comes rather from greater necessity, and 'God is three and one', predicating nothing other than God, is more necessary than 'God is to be loved supremely by the rational creature'. On the first opinion's first argument: moral science taken strictly, with every known proposition importing something in our power, is wholly practical. As transmitted by Aristotle, it contains speculative truths ('everything in the soul is a passion, power...') as principles of practical conclusions. Knowledge 'that we may become good' is practical only if its object is what makes us formally good. 'Ordered to work' as immediate directive is practical, but as a source of the directive it need not be, just as geometry guides stonemasons. Exterior actions are ordered to contemplation differently, by merit or by removing obstacles (gluttony, lust, anger), yet knowledge of them stays practical. Otherwise all moral science would be speculative. The habit of principles is ordered to conclusions without being science.
claims: Words are by convention, so the dispute over the practical intellect is largely verbal.
The intellect is one; 'speculative' and 'practical' are denominations from its habits, like 'white milk' and 'sweet milk'.
The practical intellect concerns universals as well as singulars.
Not every habit of the practical intellect is experiential.
A universal practical habit directs immediately but partially, needing knowledge of singulars.
An artisan who knows all an expert knows works as well, unless bodily habits are needed.
An equally evident speculative theological habit is nobler than a practical one.
Greater necessity confers greater nobility; 'God is triune' is more necessary than 'God is to be loved'.
Moral science strictly taken is wholly practical; as transmitted it includes speculative principles.
Ordering of exterior acts to contemplation does not make their knowledge speculative.
concepts: per se and per accidens predication

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e2153.summary: Concludes the point: whether knowledge is ordered to other knowledge makes no difference. One must consider its total and partial object, and call it speculative or practical accordingly.
claims: Whether knowledge is speculative or practical depends on its total and partial object, not on its ordering.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e2164.summary: Answers the argument that the act of love uniting the will to God is not praxis: if it is in the will's power, it is praxis. If not, as with the heaven-moving intelligence in Aristotle and with the beatific act, it is not praxis, and knowledge concerning it is not practical, since it does not direct an act that comes wholly from without. It then begins considering the case where the beatific act of love is in the will's power and so is praxis.
claims: An act of love in the will's power is praxis.
An act not in the will's power, like the beatific act, is not praxis.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e2186.summary: Even then the argument fails: beatitude would consist in both speculation (the intellect's act) and praxis (the will's act, if in its power), and the act of love would not be speculation, as willing is not understanding. Against the inference that the preceding knowledge would then be practical as that to which praxis conforms: the act is praxis, but the preceding knowledge is not practical. Incomplex knowledge of the object to be loved suffices for a voluntary act, and practical knowledge is always complex. So there is praxis without practical knowledge. An act is elicited in conformity with knowledge when it is elicited as dictated or as shown possible, which requires that the act be at least a partial object of that knowledge. Here the incomplex knowledge of the lovable object precedes the act of love (sentence continues in the next paragraph).
claims: Beatitude, if the will's act is free, consists in both speculation and praxis.
Incomplex knowledge of an object suffices for a voluntary act.
Practical knowledge is always complex.
There can be praxis without practical knowledge.
An act conforms to knowledge only if it is at least a partial object of that knowledge.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e2236.summary: So the act of love in no way terminates that act of understanding, wholly or partly, and is not elicited in conformity with it, yet it is praxis because it is in the will's power. To the next argument: happiness consists in speculation as regards the intellect's act, and in an act that is neither speculation nor praxis if fruition comes from God alone, since then it is neither an act of will nor of intellect in the relevant sense nor in the will's power. If it were in the will's power, happiness would consist in speculation and praxis. To the next: ultimate happiness as an act of understanding is speculative but includes the will's act no more than the will's act includes the intellect's. 'Speculative knowledge' means either any non-practical knowledge, complex or incomplex (in which sense happiness, the intuitive incomplex knowledge of deity, is speculative), or science of a purely speculable truth (in which sense it is not). Augustine's 'contemplative part' means the act of understanding eternal things, to which the will pertains not as essentially included but as one part belongs with another forming a unity.
claims: A free act of love can be praxis without conforming to any knowledge.
If fruition is caused by God alone, it is neither speculation nor praxis.
Happiness as intuitive knowledge of deity is speculative in the sense of non-practical.
Augustine's contemplative part includes the will only as a coordinated part.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e2300.summary: Answers the argument from metaphysics: metaphysics is not practical. Although there are naturally discoverable practical truths about God, metaphysics does not consider them. It considers only what is not in our power: that God is incorruptible, simple, everlasting, cause of all. Its truths can be principles for practical conclusions (God, as cause of all, is supremely lovable and to be honored), but those belong to some moral science. To the objection that natural speculative and practical truths about God would both belong to natural theology (metaphysics), as supernatural ones belong to our theology: extending the names 'natural theology' and 'metaphysics', one can grant that metaphysics is partly practical and moral, as our theology is. But properly metaphysics is distinguished from all moral philosophy, and philosophers and scientists speak of it so.
claims: Metaphysics considers only what about God is not in our power.
Metaphysical truths can serve as principles for practical conclusions belonging to moral science.
Properly speaking, metaphysics is distinguished from all moral philosophy.
In an extended sense, natural theology could be partly practical.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e2361.summary: Answers the argument from goodness: metaphysics considers goodness as an absolute concept common to God and creatures, by which God is distinguished from creatures. It does not consider goodness as convertible with being except when it draws a practical conclusion from speculative principles. The distinction will be explained elsewhere.
claims: Metaphysics considers goodness as an absolute common concept, not as lovability.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e2379.summary: Answers the argument from God as final cause: metaphysics considers whether God is an end, but not that he moves a rational cause that has its act in its power, since whether any creature has acts in its power belongs to the science of the soul or to moral science.
claims: Whether a creature has acts in its power belongs to psychology or ethics, not metaphysics.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e2399.summary: Answers the natural-love argument: a naturally acquired science about loving God is practical, but it does not follow that it is nobler than speculative habits. It may be less noble because what it knows is less necessary, a conclusion rather than a principle, and a principle-habit is better known. Also, a speculatively known proposition sometimes has a nobler distinguishing term than a practical one, as in 'God is the efficient cause of separated substances' versus 'God is to be adored by man'.
claims: Natural science about loving God is practical.
It need not be nobler than speculative habits.
Nobility can depend on the necessity of what is known and on the terms involved.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e2430.summary: Answers the argument that theology is not about a doable or makeable object: part of theology is not, and that part is speculative. Another part is about a partial doable object, namely truths attributing to God predicates importing our works, and that part is practical.
claims: Part of theology concerns doable objects and is practical; part does not and is speculative.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e2446.summary: Answers the argument about the practical intellect: part of theology concerns what can be otherwise, what is in our power, and that part is practical.
claims: Part of theology concerns what is in our power.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e2456.summary: Answers the second opinion's first argument: a habit about an object attainable by an operation in the knower's power, whether nobler or less noble, and having that operation as at least a partial object, is truly practical. If it is about such an object but lacks the operation as object, it is not practical. So knowing that God generates or creates the world is speculative, while knowing that God is to be obeyed or loved, that adultery is forbidden, or that parents are to be honored for God's sake is practical.
claims: A habit is practical if it has an operation in our power as at least a partial object.
Whether the operation is nobler than knowing is irrelevant.
Knowing that God creates is speculative; knowing that God is to be obeyed is practical.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e2498.summary: Answers the supporting proofs. The object relates to the knower as attainable but not as operable, so there can be speculative and practical knowledge of it, as of gold: the natural philosopher's speculative knowledge and the goldsmith's practical knowledge. Medicine and the practical sciences are practical not merely because their objects are attained by nobler operations but because they consider the operations themselves. Whether these operations are nobler than knowing is irrelevant, since mechanical artisans have practical knowledge of natural things though their operations are less noble. The confirmation is conceded for the part of theology that teaches how God is attained and deals with our works. But God is not 'operable': God is not a work but is attained through our work.
claims: One object can be known both speculatively and practically, like gold.
A science is practical because it considers operations, not because its object is reached by nobler operations.
God is not operable but is attained through our works.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e2563.summary: Answers the second (a posteriori) argument: a habit that has the act it elicits or directs as at least a partial object is practical. So part of theology is practical, since some of it has such an act as object and some does not.
claims: Part of theology has directed acts as objects and so is practical.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e2572.summary: Answers the Subtle Doctor's argument: not every part of theology is conformable to love of God. Knowledge is conformable to praxis when praxis is or can be elicited as it dictates (dictative knowledge), or, for ostensive knowledge, when praxis or its term is at least its object. Some theology has nothing operable as object. If any knowledge useful for praxis were practical, every truth would be: 'fire is hot' (useful for many operations), 'the sun warms' (so one goes into the sun). Many principles for right action come from sun, gold, fire and earth, yet there is speculative knowledge of them too. Likewise there can be speculative as well as practical knowledge of God, though God is improperly conformable to right volition.
claims: Not every part of theology is conformable to love of God.
If usefulness for action made knowledge practical, every truth would be practical.
There can be speculative and practical knowledge of the same object.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e2627.summary: Answers the confirmation: from the end come speculative as well as practical principles. Speculative principles are often prior to practical ones, and the first practical principles are conclusions deduced from speculative ones. To the first principal argument: Ockham concedes that theology is speculative in some part.
claims: Speculative principles are often prior to practical ones.
The first practical principles are deduced from speculative ones.
Theology is partly speculative.

wo8uy7-d1e203-d1e2643.summary: Answers the second principal argument: some speculative knowledge is nobler than some practical, and some practical nobler than some speculative. When one genus is nobler than another, it is not required that every member of the nobler be nobler than every member of the other, only that its noblest member be nobler than the other's noblest. To the argument for the opposite: Ockham concedes that the part of theology directing voluntary operation is practical. The paragraph closes the questions of the Prologue.
claims: Some speculative knowledge is nobler than some practical and vice versa.
One genus is nobler than another if its noblest member is nobler.
The part of theology directing voluntary operation is practical.

wo8uy7-d1e203.summary: Prologue question 12, the final question of the Prologue, asks whether the theological habit is practical or speculative. Ockham rejects the view that theology is simply speculative because it is ordered to contemplation. Theology contains simply practical truths (God is to be worshipped, the neighbor helped for God's sake), ordering to contemplation does not change a habit's character, and theology is not one science but an aggregate of really distinct habits; he rejects the 'heterogeneous single quality' alternative at length. He also rejects the views that theology is simply practical, because God is attainable by nobler operations or because, on Scotus's account, its first object virtually contains the rightness of volition. Those criteria would make every truth, even 'gold is inanimate' or metaphysics, practical. His answer: theology contains distinct cognitions, some speculative ('God is triune', 'God creates', 'the Father generates') and some practical ('God is to be loved with the whole heart', 'the Sabbath is to be kept'), depending on whether praxis or its product is a total or partial object. Answering five doubts, he holds that theological habits are distinct whether or not evident (as heretics show); that even the blessed could lack knowledge of some articles; that a habit covering speculative principles and practical conclusions is equivalently both, like wisdom; and that evident practical habits fall under science or prudence while inevident ones fall outside Aristotle's list. The speculative and practical intellect are one intellect named from its habits, like 'white milk' and 'sweet milk'. An equally evident speculative habit is nobler than a practical one, because of the greater necessity of its truths. Replies clarify that a free act of love is praxis needing only incomplex knowledge, so there is praxis without practical knowledge; that metaphysics is properly speculative; and that the nobility of genera is measured by their noblest members.
claims: Theology is neither simply speculative nor simply practical but contains distinct speculative and practical cognitions.
Knowledge is practical when praxis or its product is a total or partial object; ordering to other ends is irrelevant.
Theology is an aggregate of distinct habits, not a single heterogeneous quality.
A habit covering speculative principles and practical conclusions is equivalently both.
The speculative and practical intellect are one intellect, named from its habits.
An equally evident speculative theological habit is nobler than a practical one.
There can be praxis without practical knowledge.
Metaphysics is properly speculative.
